title: The second aorist

objectives.can: Recognise second-aorist forms by their changed stem and connect them with their present.

explanation.summary: Many of the commonest verbs form the aorist not with σα but from a different, usually shorter stem, with the endings of the imperfect. They mean the same as any other aorist; you must learn the new stem together with the present.

sections.heading: A different stem, not a different meaning
body: The first aorist (last lesson) adds σα to the stem of the verb. The second aorist does not. It uses another form of the verbal root, and the stem itself shows the tense. The two kinds are the same tense-form: both present the action as a whole, and in the indicative both are usually past. Most verbs have one or the other.

Often the aorist stem is the bare root, while the present stem has been lengthened. λαμβάνω has the aorist ἔλαβεν (stem λαβ-), βάλλω has ἔβαλεν, ἀποθνῄσκω has ἀπέθανεν, πίπτω has ἔπεσεν. Sometimes the aorist comes from a quite different root, and you simply have to learn it: λέγω has εἶπεν, ἔρχομαι has ἦλθεν, ὁράω has εἶδεν, ἐσθίω has ἔφαγεν, ἔχω has ἔσχεν. In this corpus, as in dictionaries, such verbs are filed under their present headword, so εἶπεν is a form of λέγω.

sections.heading: The endings are the imperfect's
body: The active endings of the second aorist are -ον, -ες, -ε(ν), -ομεν, -ετε, -ον, the same as the imperfect. What separates an imperfect from a second aorist is the stem. Compare ἔχω: the imperfect εἶχεν keeps the present stem, the aorist ἔσχεν has σχ-. The augment is present in both; it is the stem you check.
The aorist of γίνομαι is a middle form with the same plan: ἐγενόμην, ἐγένου, ἐγένετο, ἐγενόμεθα, ἐγένεσθε, ἐγένοντο. Its middle endings are those of the imperfect middle.

sections.heading: First-aorist endings on second-aorist stems
body: In the New Testament the plural often takes the endings of the first aorist on a second-aorist stem, especially -αν in the third person plural: ἦλθαν beside ἦλθον, εἶδαν beside εἶδον, εἶπαν beside εἶπον. Other forms of the same kind occur, such as εἶπας, εἴδαμεν, εὕραμεν and ἤλθατε. All of them are aorist indicatives of the same verbs, and you read them as such. When the ending is -αν, -α, -ας, -αμεν or -ατε but the stem is a changed one, you have met this mixture.
Do not be surprised that one verb shows both: the New Testament has εἶδον and εἶδαν, ἦλθον and ἦλθαν, as forms of the same verbs.

sections.heading: Learning the pairs
body: Because the aorist stem cannot always be guessed from the present, learn each common verb as a pair: present and aorist. The table below gives the third person singular of the aorist of fourteen verbs, each of which stands in the New Testament.

When you meet an unfamiliar form, ask three questions. Is there an augment or a prefix before it? Do the endings belong to the imperfect or the first aorist? Is the stem one you know as the aorist of some verb?

misunderstandings: A second aorist is not a 'second' event or a second kind of meaning. It is the same aorist, formed differently.
The augment alone does not tell you the tense: εἶχεν (imperfect) and ἔσχεν (aorist) both have it. Look at the stem.
An aorist with -αν in the third person plural (εἶπαν, ἦλθαν) is not a first aorist of a regular verb. The stem is the changed, second-aorist stem; only the ending is borrowed.
Do not look up εἶπεν, ἦλθεν or εἶδεν under their own spellings: dictionaries list the verbs by their present, λέγω, ἔρχομαι, ὁράω.

deeper.heading: Aorists with no thematic vowel
body: A few common second aorists have no connecting vowel before the ending: ἔγνων and ἔγνως, ἔγνω (γινώσκω), ἀνέβην and ἀνέβη (ἀναβαίνω), κατέβην and κατέβη (καταβαίνω). These belong to a small class of verbs inherited from an older stage of Greek, which you will meet again with the -μι verbs. They are grouped with the second aorists in many textbooks because they too have a root, not a σα, but their endings differ from the pattern above, so you learn them as they come.

examples.analysis: ἦλθαν and εἶδαν are second aorists of ἔρχομαι and ὁράω, third person plural, with the first-aorist ending -αν on the second-aorist stem. The tenses change in the clause: μένει is a present (the place where he is staying), ἔμειναν a first aorist (they stayed). The verse tells the story as a series of whole events.

examples.analysis: ἦλθεν (ἔρχομαι) and εἶδεν (ὁράω) are second aorists, third person singular. The son came; the father saw him. ἐπέπεσεν, 'fell upon', is also a second aorist: the prefix ἐπι- stands before the augment of the stem πεσ-, which is the aorist stem of πίπτω.

examples.analysis: ἔλαβον is a second aorist of λαμβάνω, third person plural: the stem λαβ- has no ν. ἔγνωσαν, of γινώσκω, is an aorist without a connecting vowel: the third person plural ends in -σαν directly on γνω-. ἐξῆλθον is a second aorist of ἐξέρχομαι, first person singular; the augment lengthens ε to η after the prefix ἐξ-.
